articles.title: AI Agents Should Deliver Expert Results Without Expert Prompts
articles.description: Reid Slaughter proposes pairing experts across disciplines to train AI agents to produce better work from everyday instructions.

content.text: Working in product design, AI evaluation, and Blender, I keep noticing the same problem: getting good results from an AI agent often requires knowing enough about the craft to tell it how to do the work. I can describe modeling techniques and diagnose geometry problems. A beginner with the same reference image may know exactly what they want but lack that vocabulary. AI tools should help close that expertise gap so users can describe an outcome without having to prescribe the entire process.

I’d like to test a training approach that pairs experts from different disciplines. A STEM specialist asks an agent to create a sixty second explainer video. A video specialist reviews and corrects the execution through the agent, then the STEM specialist checks that the edits preserved the facts. Recording the requests, corrections, and feedback could provide examples of how to translate everyday instructions into expert quality work. The test is whether those examples help new users get better results with less specialist intervention.

articles.title: Look Past the Flight Booking Demo
articles.description: OpenAI has a messaging problem, and I see it every time I scroll LinkedIn or Twitter(X).

content.text: OpenAI has a messaging problem, and I see it every time I scroll LinkedIn or Twitter(X).

Their demos show an AI agent booking a flight, scheduling events in a calendar, etc. People watch it, and then they argue about whether they would ever trust a bot with their travel plans. Some say they would rather book it themselves. Others list everything the agent got wrong. The threads run for hundreds of comments.
OpenAI picked flight booking because almost everyone understands it from start to finish. The demo proves that an AI can carry a messy, multi-step task all the way to the end.

OpenAI wants you to take that idea and run with it. If it can book a flight, what can it handle in your life? Maybe it can chase down an insurance claim. Maybe it can compare three contractor quotes and schedule the one that fits your budget. Maybe it can clear the tedious admin work that eats your afternoons at the office.

Many people never make that jump. They fixate on the example and stop there. I don't fully blame them. Product demos train us to read features literally. When Apple shows a camera feature, Apple wants you to use that camera feature.
AI demos work differently. The example stands in for a capability, and the audience has to do the translation. Most people won't do that work unprompted.

That makes this a marketing problem. OpenAI needs to show the extrapolation itself. Show the flight, then show three other jobs the same agent handles for three different people. Connect the dots on screen. Right now the demos ask the audience to imagine the bigger picture, and the audience keeps staring at the plane.
